prompt: An employees table has the headings emp_id, full_name, department, joined_on and holds three employees. What is one employee's entry across all four headings called?
optionA: A column
optionB: A row
optionC: A heading
optionD: A table
correctAnswerText: A row
explanation: One employee's entry across the whole width of the table is a row. It runs across the headings rather than down one of them.

prompt: In that same table, department taken all the way down the table is what?
optionA: A row
optionB: A single value
optionC: A key
optionD: A column
correctAnswerText: A column
explanation: A heading together with everything stored under it is a column. It runs down the table rather than across one employee.

prompt: Printed on paper the employees table shows a line of headings and then three employees. How many rows of data does it hold?
optionA: Three
optionB: Four, counting the headings
optionC: One
optionD: Twelve, one per value
correctAnswerText: Three
explanation: The headings name the columns and are not data, so the table holds three rows. Each employee contributes one.

prompt: The department column holds Sales, Sales and Support. What has to be true of the values in any one column?
optionA: They are all different from each other
optionB: They are always text
optionC: They are all the same kind of thing
optionD: They are stored in alphabetical order
correctAnswerText: They are all the same kind of thing
explanation: A column records one kind of thing about every row, so the values are all the same kind of thing. They may repeat, and they are not kept in any particular order.

prompt: Where in the table is one particular employee's department found?
optionA: Anywhere in the department column
optionB: Where that employee's row meets the department column
optionC: In the line of headings
optionD: In a separate table, since a department is not an employee
correctAnswerText: Where that employee's row meets the department column
explanation: A single stored value sits where a row and a column cross, so it is found where that employee's row meets the department column. Knowing only the column narrows it to a list of departments and not to one.

prompt: A table holds emp_id, full_name, email and date_of_birth. Which column is intended to serve as the key?
optionA: full_name
optionB: date_of_birth
optionC: email
optionD: emp_id
correctAnswerText: emp_id
explanation: The identifier column exists for exactly this purpose, so emp_id is the key. The others describe the employee rather than identify the row.

prompt: Two different employees are both recorded as Ana Kumar. What does that show about full_name?
optionA: It cannot be relied on to identify one row
optionB: It can, as long as the two work in different departments
optionC: It can, because the two rows have different identifiers
optionD: It can, once one of the two names is corrected
correctAnswerText: It cannot be relied on to identify one row
explanation: A value that appears twice picks out two rows rather than one, so the name cannot be relied on to identify one row. Nothing about the rest of the row repairs that.

prompt: What does a column have to do before it can be used as a key?
optionA: Hold numbers rather than text
optionB: Be the first column in the table
optionC: Pick out exactly one row, every time and forever
optionD: Be kept in sorted order
correctAnswerText: Pick out exactly one row, every time and forever
explanation: A key has one job, which is to pick out exactly one row, every time and forever. Its type and its position in the table are irrelevant to that.

prompt: In a table of forty employees, every value in date_of_birth happens to be different. Does that make it a key?
optionA: Yes; all the values being different is what a key needs
optionB: No; being different today does not make a column different in principle
optionC: Yes, as long as the column is never left blank
optionD: No; a key has to be a number
correctAnswerText: No; being different today does not make a column different in principle
explanation: The fortieth employee hired tomorrow may share a birthday with somebody already there, so being different today does not make a column different in principle. A key has to be guaranteed, not observed.

prompt: A column holds values such as 9876543210 and 0801234567. What type should it be given?
optionA: A whole number, since the values are digits
optionB: A decimal number
optionC: A date, since it is a fixed length
optionD: Text, so that a leading zero survives
correctAnswerText: Text, so that a leading zero survives
explanation: These are labels made of digits rather than quantities, and nothing is ever added to them, so the column should be text, so that a leading zero survives. Stored as a number the second value comes back shorter than it went in.

prompt: A column holds values such as 2026-04-01 and 2025-11-30. What type should it be given?
optionA: A date type
optionB: Text, since it contains dashes
optionC: A whole number, with the dashes removed
optionD: A decimal number
correctAnswerText: A date type
explanation: Stored as a date type the values can be compared and ordered as dates and invalid ones are refused. Stored as text, 2026-04-01 and 01/04/2026 would both be accepted and would not compare sensibly.

prompt: A column records whether an employee is currently active. What type should it be given?
optionA: Free text, so any wording can be used
optionB: A whole number counting the days active
optionC: A true or false type
optionD: A date type
correctAnswerText: A true or false type
explanation: There are exactly two states to record, so a true or false type fits. Free text lets Yes, yes, Y and Active all mean the same thing and none of them compare equal.

prompt: A phone column was given a whole-number type. The value 0801234 was stored and reads back as 801234. What happened?
optionA: The column was declared too short for the value
optionB: A number has no leading zero to keep, so it was never stored
optionC: The leading zero was a typing mistake by the operator
optionD: Numbers are rounded when they are stored
correctAnswerText: A number has no leading zero to keep, so it was never stored
explanation: Eight hundred and one thousand two hundred and thirty-four is the same quantity however it is written, so a number has no leading zero to keep, so it was never stored. The type was chosen because the value looked numeric rather than because it was a quantity.

prompt: A table records the customer's address on every one of their orders. The customer moves, and the address is corrected on some of their orders but not all. What is the consequence?
optionA: The table takes up more space than it needs to
optionB: Nothing goes wrong until the older orders are read
optionC: The database refuses the correction
optionD: The table now gives two different answers to the same question
correctAnswerText: The table now gives two different answers to the same question
explanation: Two stored copies now disagree, so the table now gives two different answers to the same question, and nothing in the data says which is right. Space is a side issue next to that.

prompt: While all the copies of that address still agree, why is recording it on every order already a problem?
optionA: Every future change has to reach every copy, and nothing makes sure it does
optionB: It is not a problem while the copies agree
optionC: It makes the table slower to read
optionD: It uses storage that could be saved
correctAnswerText: Every future change has to reach every copy, and nothing makes sure it does
explanation: The fault is designed in before it appears, because every future change has to reach every copy, and nothing makes sure it does. Today's agreement is luck rather than a guarantee.

prompt: authors holds 1 Rao, 2 Bose, 3 Iyer. books holds 10 Tides with author 2, 11 Reef with author 1, 12 Dunes with author 7. Who wrote Tides?
optionA: Rao
optionB: Iyer
optionC: Bose
optionD: It cannot be told from these two tables
correctAnswerText: Bose
explanation: Tides carries the identifier 2, and the author with identifier 2 is Bose. The reference is followed from the book to the author rather than the other way round.

prompt: In those same tables, Dunes refers to author 7 and no author carries that identifier. What does that tell us?
optionA: It refers to the seventh author in the list
optionB: The reference points at a row that does not exist
optionC: It records that the author is unknown
optionD: It refers to the first author, as a default
correctAnswerText: The reference points at a row that does not exist
explanation: A reference means only the row carrying that identifier, and there is no such row, so the reference points at a row that does not exist. It is not a position in the table and not a way of saying unknown.

prompt: One author may write many books, and each book has exactly one author. Which side carries the reference to the other?
optionA: Each author carries the identifiers of their books
optionB: Both sides carry a reference to the other
optionC: Neither; the two are matched on the author's name
optionD: Each book carries the identifier of its author
correctAnswerText: Each book carries the identifier of its author
explanation: A reference can hold one value, so it belongs on the side that has one thing to point at: each book carries the identifier of its author. Putting it on the author would need room for an unknown number of books.

prompt: A student may enrol on many courses, and a course may hold many students. What shape is that relationship?
optionA: Many on both sides
optionB: One student to many courses
optionC: One course to many students
optionD: One student to one course
correctAnswerText: Many on both sides
explanation: Neither side is limited to one, so the relationship is many on both sides. Describing it in one direction only leaves out half of what is true.

prompt: A designer tries to record that enrolment by adding a course column to the student row. What breaks?
optionA: Course names would be repeated across students
optionB: Nothing; a list of courses can be kept in the column
optionC: A student on three courses needs three values where there is room for one
optionD: The student table becomes too wide to print
correctAnswerText: A student on three courses needs three values where there is room for one
explanation: A single column holds one value per row, and the relationship allows many, so a student on three courses needs three values where there is room for one. Recording the pairs in a table of their own is what fits the shape.

prompt: An orders table repeats the customer's name and address on every order. Which split records each fact once?
optionA: An addresses table keyed on the address text, with orders referring to it
optionB: A customers table, with each order referring to a customer
optionC: One orders table for each city
optionD: No split; the repeated values are identical anyway
correctAnswerText: A customers table, with each order referring to a customer
explanation: The repeated facts are facts about a customer, so they belong in a customers table, with each order referring to a customer. Splitting on the address alone keeps two people at one address sharing a row they should not share.

prompt: After that split, in how many places is one customer's address recorded?
optionA: In one place per order, as before
optionB: In both tables, so either can be read on its own
optionC: Nowhere; it has to be worked out from the orders
optionD: In one place, on that customer's row
correctAnswerText: In one place, on that customer's row
explanation: The point of the split is that the fact is stored once, in one place, on that customer's row. Every order reaches it through the reference rather than keeping a copy.

prompt: A designer goes further and splits the address into separate street, city, state and country tables, each with its own identifier. Every answer the system gives stays correct. What does it cost?
optionA: A question as simple as where a customer lives now needs several tables combined
optionB: Nothing; more tables is always the better design
optionC: Addresses can no longer be corrected
optionD: The duplication comes back in a different form
correctAnswerText: A question as simple as where a customer lives now needs several tables combined
explanation: Correctness is not what suffers, which is why the stem says the answers stay right: a question as simple as where a customer lives now needs several tables combined. Splitting stops paying once the fact being separated is not independently repeated.

prompt: A bonus column is left blank both for employees who received no bonus and for employees whose bonus has not been decided yet. What has been lost?
optionA: Nothing; both cases mean the same in the end
optionB: The total, which can no longer be worked out
optionC: The difference between a bonus of nothing and a bonus not yet known
optionD: The order in which the rows were added
correctAnswerText: The difference between a bonus of nothing and a bonus not yet known
explanation: Two different situations were written down the same way, so what is lost is the difference between a bonus of nothing and a bonus not yet known. A recorded zero and a blank say different things and should not be merged.

prompt: Two rows both have nothing recorded in the same column. Are those two blanks equal to each other?
optionA: Yes; both are empty and so both are the same
optionB: No; a blank is not equal to anything, itself included
optionC: Yes, as long as the column holds text
optionD: Only when the two rows were added at the same time
correctAnswerText: No; a blank is not equal to anything, itself included
explanation: A blank stands for a value nobody knows, and two unknowns cannot be declared the same, so a blank is not equal to anything, itself included. This is why blanks have to be asked for specially rather than compared.

prompt: A manager checks a bonus report and says the reported average should equal the reported total divided by the number of employees. It does not. Both figures come from the same column, in which some rows are blank. Why do they disagree?
optionA: The average is rounded and the total is not
optionB: The total skips blanks while the average counts them as zero
optionC: The two figures are taken over different sets of rows
optionD: The average divides by the number of recorded bonuses, not by the number of employees
correctAnswerText: The average divides by the number of recorded bonuses, not by the number of employees
explanation: Both figures skip the blanks, and they differ in what the average then divides by: the average divides by the number of recorded bonuses, not by the number of employees. The manager's arithmetic silently treats every blank as a zero.

prompt: The employees table declares emp_id as its key. A new row is offered carrying an emp_id that already exists. What happens?
optionA: It is refused, because the key has to be unique
optionB: It is accepted, replacing the existing row
optionC: It is accepted, and a fresh identifier is assigned to it
optionD: It is accepted, and both rows are kept
correctAnswerText: It is refused, because the key has to be unique
explanation: A key that appeared twice would identify two rows and stop being a key, so the row is refused, because the key has to be unique. Nothing is overwritten and nothing is renumbered.

prompt: The same table declares that department_id must refer to an existing department. A new row is offered with department_id 99, and no department carries that identifier. What happens?
optionA: It is accepted, and department 99 is created
optionB: It is accepted, with the reference left blank
optionC: It is refused, because the reference points at nothing
optionD: It is accepted, and matched to the nearest existing department
correctAnswerText: It is refused, because the reference points at nothing
explanation: The constraint exists to stop exactly this row from being stored, so it is refused, because the reference points at nothing. A database does not invent the row that was referred to.

prompt: The same table also declares that full_name may not be blank. A row is offered with a fresh emp_id, a department that exists, and full_name left blank. What happens?
optionA: It is accepted, since only keys and references are enforced
optionB: It is refused, because full_name may not be blank
optionC: It is refused, because its blank duplicates another row's blank
optionD: It is accepted, and the blank is stored as empty text
correctAnswerText: It is refused, because full_name may not be blank
explanation: The first two constraints are satisfied and the third is not, so the row is refused, because full_name may not be blank. Two blanks never count as duplicates of each other, so the key constraint is not what stops it.

prompt: Rows were added to a table in a known order. Does reading the table back return them in that order?
optionA: Yes, always
optionB: Yes, unless a row has been deleted since
optionC: Yes, provided the table has a key
optionD: Not unless the reading asks for an order
correctAnswerText: Not unless the reading asks for an order
explanation: A table is a set of rows and keeps no arrival order, so the rows come back in a known order only unless the reading asks for an order. Seeing them arrive in order proves nothing about the next read.

prompt: A report read the table twice and got the rows in the same order both times. Is that order now guaranteed?
optionA: No; an order that was observed is not an order that was promised
optionB: Yes; two identical reads establish it
optionC: Yes, until the next row is added
optionD: Yes, as long as the key is numeric
correctAnswerText: No; an order that was observed is not an order that was promised
explanation: Nothing about reading a table twice creates a rule, so an order that was observed is not an order that was promised. The same read can come back differently after maintenance, a new index or a change in size.

prompt: A program takes the first row it reads to be the oldest record. It is right for eight months and then wrong, and nothing about the program changed in that time. What happened?
optionA: A row was deleted from the table
optionB: The identifier column ran out of values
optionC: The stored order changed, and it had never guaranteed anything about age
optionD: The table grew too large to read in one go
correctAnswerText: The stored order changed, and it had never guaranteed anything about age
explanation: The program depended on something that was true by accident, so the stored order changed, and it had never guaranteed anything about age. Asking for the oldest by date is what makes the answer stable.

prompt: authors holds four rows: Rao, Bose, Iyer and Nair. books holds five rows: two written by Rao, one by Bose, one by Iyer, and one referring to an author identifier that appears nowhere. Matching the two tables on the author reference gives how many rows?
optionA: Five, one for each book
optionB: Four
optionC: Nine, the two tables added
optionD: Twenty, every possible pairing
correctAnswerText: Four
explanation: Each of the four books whose author exists produces one row, and the fifth matches nothing, so four rows come back. Rao contributes two of them because Rao wrote two books.

prompt: Nair appears nowhere in that matched result, although Nair is in the authors table. Why?
optionA: Nair was removed by a condition on the result
optionB: Nair's row is missing its identifier
optionC: The matching dropped the last row of the authors table
optionD: Nair has written no book, and matching keeps only rows that pair up
correctAnswerText: Nair has written no book, and matching keeps only rows that pair up
explanation: Matching produces a row only where the two sides correspond, so Nair has written no book, and matching keeps only rows that pair up. An author with no books and a book with no author drop out for the same reason.

prompt: A report counts employees for each department and the counts add up to more than the number of employees. Every employee belongs to exactly one department. What explains it?
optionA: Something else joined into the report repeats each employee across several rows
optionB: Some employees have no department recorded
optionC: The line of headings is being counted as a row
optionD: Each department is being counted twice
correctAnswerText: Something else joined into the report repeats each employee across several rows
explanation: The stem rules out an employee belonging to two departments, so the extra rows come from elsewhere: something else joined into the report repeats each employee across several rows. An employee with three recorded skills is counted three times.

prompt: A similar report totals fewer employees than the table holds. The report keeps only rows where the department reference matches a department row. What explains the shortfall?
optionA: Some employees are counted twice and the total was corrected
optionB: The count is being rounded down
optionC: Some employees refer to a department that no longer exists and so match nothing
optionD: The departments table holds more rows than it should
correctAnswerText: Some employees refer to a department that no longer exists and so match nothing
explanation: Rows that fail to match are left out entirely rather than reported as unmatched, so some employees refer to a department that no longer exists and so match nothing. Missing employees and repeated employees are opposite symptoms of two different faults.

prompt: A design records only each customer's current balance. Somebody later asks how much that customer spent last month. Can the design answer?
optionA: Yes, by subtracting last month's balance from this month's
optionB: No; the individual amounts were never written down
optionC: Yes, if the balance carries the date it was last changed
optionD: Yes, from the customers table alone
correctAnswerText: No; the individual amounts were never written down
explanation: Only the running figure was kept and every amount that changed it was discarded, so no; the individual amounts were never written down. Last month's balance is not stored either, which is why the subtraction has nothing to work from.

prompt: A design stores a customer's several phone numbers in one column, separated by commas. Every screen in the system displays them correctly. What can the design not do?
optionA: Show the numbers to a user
optionB: Hold more than two numbers in the column
optionC: Be read by a program at all
optionD: Answer a question about one number, such as which customers share a number
correctAnswerText: Answer a question about one number, such as which customers share a number
explanation: Display works because the whole column is shown at once, which is why nothing looks wrong: what it cannot do is answer a question about one number, such as which customers share a number. The database sees one piece of text rather than several values.

prompt: What kind of question can a design never answer, when it records only the state a thing is in now?
optionA: Any question about how that state was arrived at, or what it was before
optionB: Any question about the present state
optionC: Questions that need more than one table
optionD: Questions that need a total rather than a list
correctAnswerText: Any question about how that state was arrived at, or what it was before
explanation: The present is exactly what such a design keeps, and everything else has been thrown away, so it can never answer any question about how that state was arrived at, or what it was before. The question usually arrives long after the design is in use.

prompt: Recording every change as it happens, as well as the value it produced, answers a wider range of later questions. What does it cost?
optionA: Nothing; it is the better design in every respect
optionB: The current value becomes impossible to find
optionC: Many more rows, and the current value now has to be worked out or kept in step separately
optionD: The table can no longer have a key
correctAnswerText: Many more rows, and the current value now has to be worked out or kept in step separately
explanation: The extra questions are paid for with many more rows, and the current value now has to be worked out or kept in step separately. That second copy is itself a duplication that has to be maintained.

prompt: A design is being settled while the questions it will have to answer are still unknown. What is the safer default?
optionA: Record the summaries, since those are what people actually ask for
optionB: Record the facts as they happen, and work summaries out from them later
optionC: Record both the facts and the summaries in the same column
optionD: Postpone the design until the questions are known
correctAnswerText: Record the facts as they happen, and work summaries out from them later
explanation: A summary can always be produced from the facts and the facts can never be recovered from a summary, so record the facts as they happen, and work summaries out from them later. The asymmetry is what makes this the default rather than a preference.

prompt: A monthly report totals the sales for a month in which no sale was made. The report shows a blank where the total should be, and does not fail. What is the reason?
optionA: The report failed and printed nothing
optionB: The whole sales table is empty
optionC: That month was left out of the report
optionD: A total over no rows has no value to report, unless the report supplies one
correctAnswerText: A total over no rows has no value to report, unless the report supplies one
explanation: There was nothing to add, and adding nothing yields no figure at all: a total over no rows has no value to report, unless the report supplies one. The absence of a failure is the clue that this is normal behaviour rather than a fault.

prompt: For that same empty month the report shows a count of 0 next to a blank total, and both figures are correct. What should the reader take from the pair?
optionA: That no sale was recorded at all, rather than sales that came to nothing
optionB: That the report is inconsistent with itself
optionC: That the total failed while the count succeeded
optionD: That the count is wrong and should also be blank
correctAnswerText: That no sale was recorded at all, rather than sales that came to nothing
explanation: The two figures answer different questions and agree with each other: no sale was recorded at all, rather than sales that came to nothing. A zero total would have been the wrong claim to print.

prompt: A list of departments with the number of employees in each leaves out one department entirely. That department currently has nobody in it. Why is it missing?
optionA: It was removed by a condition somewhere in the report
optionB: Its identifier is missing from the departments table
optionC: Matching produces no row at all for a department with nobody to match
optionD: Counts of zero are dropped when the report is formatted
correctAnswerText: Matching produces no row at all for a department with nobody to match
explanation: The report is built by pairing departments with employees, and matching produces no row at all for a department with nobody to match. The department is absent rather than shown as zero.

prompt: How is that empty department made to appear in the list, showing a count of zero?
optionA: Add a placeholder employee to the empty department
optionB: Keep every department, and count only the employees that match each one
optionC: Count the rows of the departments table instead
optionD: Remove the condition that limits which employees are counted
correctAnswerText: Keep every department, and count only the employees that match each one
explanation: The department has to survive the matching before it can be counted, so keep every department, and count only the employees that match each one. The count then comes out as zero rather than as a missing line.

prompt: Rather than change the report, somebody adds one placeholder employee to each empty department so that every department appears. The list now looks right. What does that cost?
optionA: Nothing; the placeholders are ignored by everything else
optionB: The report becomes slower to produce
optionC: The departments table has to be given new identifiers
optionD: The employees table now holds rows describing nobody, and every count of employees is wrong
correctAnswerText: The employees table now holds rows describing nobody, and every count of employees is wrong
explanation: The fix is applied to the data rather than to the report, so the employees table now holds rows describing nobody, and every count of employees is wrong. Every future reader has to know about the placeholders, and eventually one will not.

prompt: Four columns are proposed as the key of a customers table: the email address, the phone number, the full name, and a number the system assigns. All four hold different values in today's data. Which should be chosen?
optionA: The number the system assigns, because nothing outside the system can change it
optionB: The email address, which is unique and already known
optionC: The phone number, which is unique and shorter
optionD: The full name, combined with the city to make it unique
correctAnswerText: The number the system assigns, because nothing outside the system can change it
explanation: Uniqueness today is the one thing all four have, so the choice turns on what happens next: the number the system assigns, because nothing outside the system can change it. The other three belong to the customer, who is entitled to change them.

prompt: The email address was chosen as the key, and a customer now changes their email address. What has to happen?
optionA: Nothing; the change affects only the customer's own row
optionB: The customer has to be recorded again as a new customer
optionC: Every row anywhere that refers to that customer by email has to be found and changed too
optionD: The old address has to be kept forever alongside the new one
correctAnswerText: Every row anywhere that refers to that customer by email has to be found and changed too
explanation: A key is copied into every row that refers to the customer, so every row anywhere that refers to that customer by email has to be found and changed too. Missing one of them silently detaches part of the customer's history.

prompt: The phone number was chosen as the key, and two people in one household share a landline. What happens when the second person is recorded?
optionA: Both rows are stored and the key stops being enforced
optionB: The second row is refused, and the two people cannot both be held in the table
optionC: The second row replaces the first
optionD: The number is stored twice and a warning is issued
correctAnswerText: The second row is refused, and the two people cannot both be held in the table
explanation: The key constraint does exactly what it was declared to do, so the second row is refused, and the two people cannot both be held in the table. A value that is unique for most people is not a key.

prompt: Why is a system-assigned key preferred, even though it stores a value that means nothing to anybody outside the system?
optionA: It takes up less room than an address or a name
optionB: It can be sorted more quickly than text
optionC: It prevents the same person being recorded twice
optionD: It is never asked to change, which is the one property a key needs and real values lack
correctAnswerText: It is never asked to change, which is the one property a key needs and real values lack
explanation: Meaning is not what a key is for: it is never asked to change, which is the one property a key needs and real values lack. It does nothing at all to stop the same person being entered twice, which is a separate problem.
